name: AC wattage
seoDesc: AC wattage: work out voltage from the power factor and the wattage. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: voltage is what the AC wattage calculator works out, and it gets there from the power factor and the wattage. Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the AC wattage calculator work?
sections.html:
The AC wattage calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports voltage in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the current type and the type of three phase); then you type in the power factor, the wattage and the wattage (2).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as AC single phase and AC three phase. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as line-to-line and line-to-neutral. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in watts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in watts. The unit chip switches it to any of the 21 supported units.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the AC wattage calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Voltage=wattage ÷ (current × power factor)
Voltage=(1 ÷ 3) × the square root of (3) × wattage ÷ (current × power factor)
Voltage=(1 ÷ 3) × wattage ÷ (current × power factor)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Current type set to AC single phase, Type of three phase set to line-to-line, Current = 10 A and Power factor = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Voltage = 0.1 V and Wattage = 17.3205 W.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Voltage = 0.1 V and Wattage = 17.3205 W should be roughly the size you expected from Current type set to AC single phase and Type of three phase set to line-to-line.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in volts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in amperes, and convertible to any of the 3 units on that chip.
  • Shown in watts, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Voltage, opening in volts
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes
  • Power, opening in watts
  • Power, opening in watts
  • Power, opening in watts

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The AC wattage calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the power factor and the wattage — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the AC wattage calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns voltage, derived from the power factor and the wattage. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the AC wattage calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the power factor and the wattage, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter voltage in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Voltage opens in volts and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Voltage = 0.1 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the AC wattage calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
